questions.prompt: What is the Salesforce Certified Technical Architect (CTA) credential's exam format called, in which a candidate designs a solution to a scenario and defends it live before a panel of existing CTAs?
options: A standard 60-question multiple-choice exam
An Architect Review Board
A Trailhead Superbadge
An open-book take-home assignment
A peer code review
A written essay exam
questions.explain: The CTA credential is earned through a two-step Architect Review Board: an evaluation of prerequisites and experience, then a review board exam where the candidate designs a solution to a scenario and defends it live before a panel of CTAs.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes a standard certification exam format, which is not how the CTA credential is earned — unlike most Salesforce certifications, the CTA is earned through a live, scenario-based review board rather than a multiple-choice test.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for "a dashboard showing at-risk deals." Applying the why-ladder technique, what is the architect actually trying to uncover?
options: The exact chart colors the stakeholder prefers
Whether the stakeholder is authorized to make requests
The real underlying business driver behind the stated request, which might be served by a different solution than a dashboard
The specific field-level security needed for the dashboard
questions.explain: The why-ladder pushes past the first stated request, asking why it matters repeatedly, until the real business driver surfaces — which might end up being served by an entirely different solution than the one originally proposed.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce architect credential to its actual domain focus.
right: The capstone credential earned via an Architect Review Board
Off-platform systems, integration, and identity/access between systems
Native platform depth: data modeling, sharing, and application design
questions.explain: System Architect focuses on off-platform systems, integration, and identity/access between systems. Application Architect focuses on native platform depth: data modeling, sharing, and application design. Both feed into the CTA, the capstone credential earned through an Architect Review Board rather than a standard exam.

questions.prompt: Put these five stages of the solution design process in the correct order.
questions.explain: The process runs clarify, explore, evaluate, decide, validate — confirming the real requirement first, surfacing real alternatives before narrowing, weighing them against constraints, recording the decision and reasoning, then confirming the chosen design with stakeholders before real implementation time is spent.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that describes a genuine architect mindset habit from this course, rather than a mistake to avoid.
options: Asking "under what conditions does this stop working?" right after confirming a design works
Presenting a chosen design as having no downside at all
Naming your own design's weakest point before a reviewer finds it
Designing for every hypothetical future requirement regardless of whether it's been stated
Distinguishing a stated future requirement from a merely possible one
questions.explain: The genuine habits are: asking what would break a working design, surfacing your own design's weak point before a reviewer does, and distinguishing a real stated future requirement from a merely hypothetical one. Hiding a design's downside and over-engineering for imaginary futures are exactly the mistakes this course warns against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Salesforce ________ Architect credential focuses on off-platform systems, integration, and identity/access between systems.
questions.explain: The System Architect credential is specifically focused on what happens outside the core platform: integration, identity and access between systems, and deployment governance — distinct from Application Architect's native-platform focus.

questions.prompt: A go-live date set by a board commitment is best described as which of these, per this course's definitions?
options: A constraint, since it's fixed and not up for negotiation
An assumption, since it might change
A risk, since it might not be met
An open question, since it hasn't been resolved yet
questions.explain: A constraint is something fixed about the problem that the design has to work within, like a board-committed go-live date — it isn't negotiated away by good design, unlike an assumption, which is merely believed true until verified.

questions.prompt: Match each risk category to the scenario that best illustrates it.
right: A design that depends on another system's availability or documented behavior
A design that works cleanly at today's volume but might behave very differently at real scale
A design where one shared integration user failing takes down every integration depending on it
A design assuming users will adopt a new process correctly without training or habit conflict
questions.explain: Data volume risk is about behavior at scale. Integration dependency risk is about relying on another system's availability. Change-management risk is about user adoption. Single point of failure risk is about one shared component whose failure takes everything down with it.

questions.prompt: Put these four parts of presenting a design decision in the order this course teaches them.
items: State the decision itself in one sentence
State the one or two factors that actually drove the decision
Name the alternative that was considered and why it lost
Name the decision's main known weakness or risk
questions.explain: Stating the decision first lets the audience know what's being proposed before following the reasoning. Then the key drivers, then the rejected alternative and why it lost, and finally the decision's main known weakness — giving the audience everything needed to push back on something specific.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the MoSCoW prioritization method, the M stands for ________ have.
questions.explain: MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must, Should, Could, and Won't have (this time) — Must have meaning the solution fails its core purpose without it.

questions.prompt: Select every section this course says a usable architecture blueprint should include.
options: Context and objective
Scope
Design overview
A complete list of every employee at the company
Open questions
questions.explain: A usable blueprint covers context/objective, scope, a design overview, key decisions and trade-offs, constraints and assumptions, risks, and open questions — not an unrelated company directory.

questions.prompt: What does "authentication" mean, as distinct from "authorization"?
options: Determining what an already-identified user is allowed to do
Establishing who a user actually is
A synonym for a Federation ID
The process of granting a permission set to a user
questions.explain: Authentication establishes who a user actually is. Authorization is a separate, later question: what that already-identified user is allowed to do.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes authorization, not authentication — authorization answers what an authenticated user can do, while authentication answers who that user actually is in the first place, a distinct and earlier question.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce record-access layer to what it actually does.
right: Opens access upward automatically through the management structure
Sharing one specific record with one specific user for a one-off situation
The baseline per-object setting; the only layer that can actually restrict access
Automatic criteria- or ownership-based exceptions that widen access for a defined group
questions.explain: OWD is the baseline floor and the only layer that can actually restrict access. The role hierarchy opens access upward automatically. Sharing rules widen access for a defined group based on criteria or ownership. Manual sharing is the most granular, one-off grant.

questions.prompt: Put these four record-access layers in order from the broadest floor to the most granular, one-off grant.
questions.explain: OWD sets the baseline floor every other layer builds on. The role hierarchy adds vertical visibility automatically. Sharing rules add defined-group exceptions. Manual sharing is the most granular, one-off layer, reserved for situations that don't deserve a standing rule.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce integration patterns, per this course.
options: A synchronous integration blocks the caller until a response is received
Fire and Forget waits for the remote process to fully complete before continuing
Data virtualization reads external data live instead of storing a copy in Salesforce
Batch Data Synchronization is typically used for larger volumes where some delay in freshness is acceptable
Salesforce's own guidance recommends choosing the technology before the integration pattern
questions.explain: Synchronous calls block until a response arrives. Data virtualization reads external data live rather than storing a copy. Batch synchronization fits larger volumes with acceptable delay. Fire and Forget specifically does NOT wait for completion, and Salesforce's guidance recommends choosing the pattern before the technology, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: A company has two business units with nearly identical sales processes and no regulatory separation requirement. Per this course's framing, what's the reasonable default system architecture approach?
options: Split into two orgs immediately, since isolation is always safer
Multi-org always costs less than single-org at any scale
Org limits never matter to this decision
Start with one org, since no specific, named reason justifies the added integration and governance cost of splitting
questions.explain: Absent a hard separation need, starting with one org and only splitting for a specific, named reason is the reasonable default, since under-splitting is usually cheaper than paying permanent integration overhead for a separation nobody actually needed.

questions.prompt: What does this course mean by solution architecture being a "cross-cutting practice" rather than a sixth domain?
options: It has no relationship to the other five domains
It is simply another name for data architecture
It balances trade-offs across all five domains for one specific solution, rather than being its own separate technical subject
It only applies when no security requirements exist
questions.explain: Solution architecture doesn't have its own isolated body of technical knowledge the way data or security architecture does — it's the practice of finding a design that balances trade-offs across all five domains for one real solution.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce environment type to its typical use.
right: The closest replica of production, used for final staging and performance testing
Metadata only, used for individual day-to-day feature coding
Disposable, source-configured environment, not a traditional sandbox
Metadata plus a configured sample of production data, used for integration/UAT testing
questions.explain: Developer sandboxes fit everyday individual feature coding. Partial Copy sandboxes fit integration/UAT testing with realistic sample data. Full sandboxes are the closest replica of production, reserved for final staging and performance testing. Scratch orgs aren't sandboxes at all — they're disposable, source-configured environments common in DX-based pipelines.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a strong executive brief covers what's proposed, the cost of saying yes, and the cost of saying ________.
questions.explain: A strong executive brief fits in roughly three sentences: what's being proposed, what it costs the business to say yes, and what it costs to say no — the risk or opportunity cost of not proceeding.

questions.prompt: Why does this course say the CTA Architect Review Board format relies on skills built in this course, even though this course isn't itself CTA exam prep?
options: Because the review board's presentation-and-defend format relies directly on this course's decision structure, risk framing, and audience-reading skills
Because the review board only tests memorized trivia unrelated to communication
Because this course is a complete substitute for all review board preparation
Because communication skills are irrelevant to how the review board is scored
questions.explain: The review board's challenge-and-defend format draws directly on skills this course built — the four-part decision structure, constraints/assumptions and risk framing, and reading an audience — even though scenario-specific exam drilling comes later in the path.
